question:
Passage: A constitution is often imagined as a fence — a list of things the state may not do to those it governs. On this familiar picture, liberty lives in the gaps the fence leaves open, and the citizen is free to the precise extent that the law falls silent. Yet this account, for all its appeal, mistakes the part for the whole. The same document that restrains power also constitutes it: it creates the offices, defines the procedures, and confers the very authority whose excesses it then limits. Without the constitution there would be no lawful power to fence in, only the unstructured force of whoever happened to be strongest.

Seen this way, the rule of law is not merely a brake but an engine. Its deepest function is not to leave individuals alone but to make collective action possible on terms that do not collapse into the rule of the powerful. A society governed by stable, public, prospective rules can coordinate the plans of millions of strangers who will never meet, precisely because each can rely on the rules holding tomorrow as they held today. Predictability, not permission, is the currency of freedom here.

It follows that the gravest threat to liberty is not always the law that forbids too much, but the arbitrariness that forbids unpredictably — the power that may be exercised today and withheld tomorrow for no reason that can be stated in advance. A citizen subject to such a power is unfree even if, as it happens, the power is never used against her; for she must live as a supplicant, anticipating a will she cannot foresee. Liberty, on this understanding, is less the silence of the law than the constancy of it.

Question: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?
options: (a) A constitution's only purpose is to restrain the state by listing what it may not do.
(b) The rule of law secures freedom less by leaving people alone than by replacing arbitrary power with stable, predictable rules.
(c) Liberty exists only in the areas where the law happens to be silent.
(d) Citizens are free only when the state never exercises any of its powers.
explanation: The passage reframes liberty as the constancy/predictability of law that replaces arbitrary power, explicitly rejecting the 'silence of the law' view. (a)/(c) are the partial view it corrects; (d) is contradicted by 'unfree even if the power is never used.'

question:
Passage: We tend to treat forgetting as memory's failure — a leak in a vessel meant to hold everything. The ideal mind, on this view, would forget nothing, recording each face, fact and afternoon in perfect and permanent detail. But a mind that forgot nothing would not be a better mind; it would be a paralysed one. To think at all is to generalise, and to generalise is to let go of particulars. The reader who remembered every individual letter would never arrive at the word; the traveller who retained every blade of grass would never recognise the meadow.

Forgetting, then, is not the opposite of memory but one of its instruments. By discarding the incidental, the mind clears space for the pattern; by loosening its grip on the exact, it gains the power to recognise the similar. What looks like loss is often a kind of editing — a continual sifting that keeps the useful near the surface and lets the irrelevant sink. Memory that did not forget would not be richer; it would be a featureless archive in which nothing could be found because nothing had been judged worth finding.

This is why the rare individuals who cannot forget are so often tormented rather than gifted. Buried under the undifferentiated weight of everything that ever happened to them, they struggle to abstract, to compare, to move on. Their predicament suggests that the economy of the mind depends not on retaining the most but on retaining the right things — and that the discipline of forgetting is, paradoxically, a condition of understanding.

Question: Which of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: (a) Forgetting is a constructive instrument of thought that enables generalisation and understanding, not merely a defect of memory.
(b) The ideal mind would retain every detail it ever encountered.
(c) People who cannot forget enjoy a clear cognitive advantage over others.
(d) Memory and forgetting are wholly unrelated mental processes.
explanation: The thesis is that forgetting is 'one of memory's instruments' and 'a condition of understanding.' (b)/(c) are views the passage rejects; (d) contradicts 'not the opposite of memory but one of its instruments.'

question:
Passage: Every medium that competes for human attention must eventually discover the same truth: attention is finite, and what captures it most reliably is not what serves us best. The eye is drawn to motion, the mind to novelty, the heart to outrage; and a system that succeeds by capturing attention will, if left to optimise without restraint, drift inexorably toward the motion, the novelty and the outrage, whatever their cost to the person on the other side of the screen. This is not the result of any single designer's malice. It is the logic of the competition itself, which rewards whatever holds the gaze and is blind to whatever nourishes the mind.

The danger is subtle because the system gives us, at every moment, exactly what we asked for. Each click is freely made; each is, in the small, a satisfaction. Yet the sum of these satisfactions can be a life we would not have chosen — hours dissolved, attention fragmented, the capacity for sustained thought quietly eroded. We are not coerced; we are courted, and then slowly remade in the image of what most easily holds us.

To say this is not to counsel despair but to locate responsibility correctly. If the pull toward distraction is structural, then resisting it cannot be merely a matter of individual willpower, any more than one swimmer's effort can change the direction of a tide. The remedy, if there is one, must be partly architectural: a redesign of the systems themselves, and of the incentives that shape them, so that what captures our attention bears some honest relation to what deserves it.

Question: Which of the following best captures the main argument of the passage?
options: (a) Attention-capturing systems naturally tend to serve users' deepest interests.
(b) Individual self-discipline is, by itself, fully sufficient to overcome digital distraction.
(c) The designers of these systems act mainly out of deliberate malice.
(d) Because attention-driven systems are structurally biased toward what grips us rather than what benefits us, reducing distraction requires changing the systems, not just individual willpower.
explanation: The passage argues the bias is structural ('the logic of the competition') and the remedy 'must be partly architectural.' (a) is contradicted; (b) is rejected ('cannot be merely a matter of individual willpower'); (c) is explicitly denied ('not the result of any single designer's malice').

question:
Passage: When a technology for copying words cheaply appeared in the towns of fifteenth-century Europe, its first effect was not the one we now remember. Printing did not immediately enlighten; it multiplied. Whatever was being copied — wisdom or error, devotion or slander — could now travel further and faster than before, and the early presses poured out almanacs and pardons as readily as the works we have since chosen to celebrate. A tool for spreading ideas spreads whatever ideas it is given; it has no preference of its own.

What the press changed was less the content of thought than its conditions. Once a text could be reproduced identically in a thousand copies, knowledge ceased to be the fragile possession of those who guarded the manuscripts. A claim made in one city could be checked, contested and built upon in another; errors that had quietly propagated through generations of hand-copying could at last be caught by comparison. The press did not make people wiser, but it made wisdom — and folly — cumulative in a way they had not been before.

The lesson is not that the technology was neutral, for it was not: by making copies cheap and identical, it favoured certain habits of mind — comparison, correction, the patient accumulation of small improvements. But it favoured them only as a riverbed favours a river. It set the conditions within which a slow transformation could occur, while leaving to human beings the long labour of actually bringing it about.

Question: Which of the following best states the central idea of the passage?
options: (a) By making texts cheap and identical, printing reshaped the conditions of knowledge - enabling comparison and cumulative correction - without itself making people wiser.
(b) Printing instantly enlightened the societies that adopted it.
(c) The printing press was a perfectly neutral tool with no influence on thought.
(d) The press served mainly to spread error rather than knowledge.
explanation: The passage argues the press changed 'the conditions of thought,' favouring comparison and correction, yet 'did not make people wiser.' (b) contradicts 'did not immediately enlighten'; (c) contradicts 'the technology was [not] neutral'; (d) overstates - it spread both wisdom and folly.

question:
Passage: We like to believe that a person can be judged only for what lies within his control. Praise and blame, on this comfortable principle, should track the will alone — the choices made, the intentions formed — and never the accidents of circumstance that the agent did not author. Two drivers equally careless, equally distracted, deserve, it seems, the same reproach; that one of them happened upon a child in the road and the other an empty street is, on this view, a difference in luck, not in guilt.

And yet our actual judgments stubbornly refuse to honour the principle. We do not, in fact, blame the two drivers equally; the one who caused a death is treated, by the law and by his own conscience alike, as having done something far graver, though his carelessness was no greater. The same act of negligence is a minor lapse or a tragedy depending on a swerve of fortune entirely outside the agent's hands. We seem committed both to the principle that luck should not affect moral standing and to a practice that lets it affect that standing profoundly.

The discomfort this produces is not a mere confusion to be tidied away. It points to something genuine about moral life: that we are not the sealed authors of our actions but creatures embedded in a world we do not control, whose deeds acquire their meaning partly from consequences we did not choose. To insist that only the will may be judged is to picture a self that does not exist — a will floating free of the world in which alone it can act.

Question: Which of the following best captures the central concern of the passage?
options: (a) People should always be judged solely by their intentions.
(b) Our moral judgments are in tension with the principle that only what is within our control should affect moral standing, revealing that outcomes shaped by luck do affect that standing.
(c) The two drivers are in fact equally blameworthy in every respect.
(d) Luck plays no role at all in how we actually assign blame.
explanation: The passage highlights the tension between the control principle and our actual practice, concluding that luck does affect moral standing. (a) is the principle being problematised; (c)/(d) contradict the practice the author describes.

question:
Passage: Imagine a pasture open to all, on which each herdsman may graze as many animals as he wishes. For any one herder, the logic is plain: each additional animal he adds yields him its full value, while the cost of the slightly worsened pasture is shared among everyone who uses it. So he adds another, and another — and so, reasoning identically, does every other herder. Each behaves rationally by his own lights; together they destroy the very pasture on which all depend. The ruin is not the work of villains but of ordinary people following incentives that point, individually, in exactly the wrong collective direction.

What makes such situations hard is that exhortation does not touch their cause. Telling each herder to restrain himself asks him to bear a certain private cost for a benefit that, if others do not also restrain themselves, will not materialise — and that, if others do restrain themselves, he can enjoy without any sacrifice of his own. The conscientious are thus penalised and the free riders rewarded, which is precisely the wrong arrangement of incentives for the outcome we want.

The way out, where one exists, rarely lies in expecting people to act against their interests. It lies in changing the interests themselves — by assigning rights, setting shared limits, or binding everyone to rules that make restraint individually sensible because others are bound to it too. The problem is not that people are bad but that the structure is, and structures, unlike characters, can be redesigned.

(b) When individuals rationally pursuing private gain share the cost of a common resource, it tends to be overused; the remedy lies in restructuring incentives rather than in moral exhortation.
(c) Moral exhortation is the most effective way to protect common resources.
(d) Rational self-interest always leads to the best collective outcomes.
explanation: The passage diagnoses a structural incentive problem ('the structure is [bad]') solved by redesigning incentives, not exhortation. (a) is denied ('not the work of villains'); (c) is rejected; (d) is the opposite of the passage's point.

question:
Passage: The official map of a great city — its zoning plans, its registered businesses, its tax rolls — captures only a fraction of the life actually lived within it. Alongside the formal economy of contracts and licences runs a vast informal one: the street vendor without a permit, the home workshop off the books, the network of unrecorded loans and unwritten tenancies through which much of the city's poor majority actually survives. Planners have often regarded this shadow economy as a problem to be cleared away — a sign of disorder, backwardness, a failure of the city to become fully modern.

But to treat informality merely as the absence of order is to misread it. The unlicensed market is not the lack of a system; it is a different system, with its own rules, reputations and enforcement, often more responsive to the needs of the poor than the formal channels that exclude them. When the licensed alternative is too costly, too slow or too out of reach for those at the bottom, the informal arrangement is not a deviation from how the city works but a large part of how it works at all. To bulldoze it in the name of order can destroy the only economy the poor can actually participate in, replacing a messy functioning system with a tidy non-functioning one.

This does not mean informality should be romanticised; it can also trap people in insecurity, without the protections that formal status confers. The point is rather that the choice is not between order and disorder but between two kinds of order — and that policy which fails to see the hidden one will keep mistaking the city's survival mechanisms for its diseases.

Question: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?
options: (a) Informality is not the absence of order but a different order, often serving the poor where formal channels fail; policy that ignores this misjudges it.
(b) The informal economy is pure disorder that cities should eliminate.
(c) The informal economy should be romanticised as superior to the formal one.
(d) Official maps capture the full life actually lived in a city.
explanation: The thesis is that informality is 'not the lack of a system; it is a different system,' with a warning that policy must see 'the hidden one.' (b)/(d) are contradicted; (c) is explicitly rejected ('should [not] be romanticised').

question:
Passage: A translation is often judged by a single demand: that it be faithful to the original. But faithful to what? A sentence in any living language carries more than its dictionary meaning. It carries rhythm, connotation, the weight of what is customary to say and the surprise of what is not — a whole atmosphere that clings to words in their native setting and evaporates the moment they are lifted out. The translator who renders only the literal sense, matching word to word with mechanical care, produces something accurate and dead: a body without breath. Fidelity to the words can be a betrayal of the meaning.

So the translator is forced into a kind of double loyalty that can never be perfectly honoured. To carry across the music and the feeling, she must sometimes depart from the letter; to keep faith with the letter, she must sometimes sacrifice the music. There is no formula that resolves this, no setting at which the dial can rest. Every choice gains something and loses something, and the translator's art lies precisely in judging, again and again, which loss is the more bearable.

This is why translation, far from being a mechanical substitution, is one of the most demanding forms of reading. The translator must understand the original more deeply than an ordinary reader does — must feel not only what it says but how it means — and then perform the near-impossible feat of saying something that is at once another text and the same one. That the task cannot be completed perfectly is not a mark of its failure but of its seriousness: it is hard precisely because there is so much, beyond mere words, to be kept.

Question: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: (a) Translation is a demanding interpretive art requiring judgment between competing loyalties - to the letter and to the meaning - that no formula can resolve.
(b) A good translation is simply a word-for-word rendering of the original.
(c) Translation is impossible and ought not to be attempted.
(d) The literal meaning of words is all that a translator needs to preserve.
explanation: The passage argues that fidelity is double and unformulaic, making translation 'one of the most demanding forms of reading.' (b)/(d) are the mechanical view rejected; (c) overstates - it is hard, not pointless.

question: In a certain code, 'A @ B' means A is greater than or equal to B; 'A # B' means A is less than or equal to B; 'A & B' means A is greater than B; 'A % B' means A is less than B. Given the statements P & Q, Q @ R and R # S, which of the following is definitely true?
explanation: P > Q and Q >= R give P > R, i.e. 'P & R' is definitely true. The link R <= S breaks the chain, so comparisons of P or Q with S are indeterminate, and 'R @ P' is false.
subject: CSAT

question: Pointing to a photograph, a woman said, 'He is the only son of the mother of my brother's sister.' How is the man in the photograph related to the woman?
explanation: 'My brother's sister' shares the woman's own mother; the only son of that mother is the woman's brother. Hence the man is her brother.
subject: CSAT

question: A man walks 10 m towards the north, turns right and walks 10 m, turns right again and walks 20 m, then turns right and walks 10 m. In which direction and how far is he now from his starting point?
explanation: Taking the start as origin, the successive points are (0,10), (10,10), (10,-10), (0,-10). The final point (0,-10) is 10 m due south of the start.
subject: CSAT

question: Find the next term of the series: 3, 6, 11, 18, 27, ?
explanation: The differences are 3, 5, 7, 9 (consecutive odd numbers); the next difference is 11, giving 27 + 11 = 38.
subject: CSAT

question: Find the next term of the series: B2, D4, G7, K11, ?
explanation: The letters are at positions 2, 4, 7, 11 (gaps of +2, +3, +4), so the next is position 16 = P; the number equals the letter's position, giving P16.
subject: CSAT

question: If 1 January 2024 is a Monday, what day of the week is 1 January 2025?
explanation: 2024 is a leap year (366 days); 366 mod 7 = 2 odd days, so the day advances by two from Monday to Wednesday.
subject: CSAT

question: In a certain code, 'CAT' is written as 'DBU' and 'DOG' as 'EPH'. How is 'LION' written in that code?
explanation: Each letter is shifted forward by one. L->M, I->J, O->P, N->O, giving MJPO.
subject: CSAT

question: Cobbler is related to Shoes in the same way as Mason is related to:
explanation: A cobbler's finished product is shoes; a mason's is a wall. Bricks and cement are materials and a hammer is a tool, not the product.
subject: CSAT

question: Find the odd one out: 8, 27, 64, 100, 125.
explanation: 8, 27, 64 and 125 are the perfect cubes 2^3, 3^3, 4^3 and 5^3; 100 is not a perfect cube.
subject: CSAT

question: Statement (office notice): 'Please switch off the lights and fans before leaving the room.' Which of the following is/are implicit assumption(s)? (1) Employees may otherwise forget to switch them off. (2) Leaving lights and fans running wastes electricity.
explanation: The notice presupposes that employees might leave the appliances on (1) and that doing so is wasteful enough to warn against (2); both underlie the instruction.
subject: CSAT

question: Statement: Should the use of single-use plastic carry-bags be banned in the country? Argument I: Yes, non-biodegradable plastic causes serious long-term environmental damage. Argument II: No, because some other countries still allow plastic bags. Which argument is strong?
explanation: Argument I addresses a substantive, relevant harm and is strong; argument II is a weak appeal to what other countries do, which is irrelevant to whether a ban is desirable here.
subject: CSAT

question: Statements: (I) No artist is a coward. (II) All dancers are artists. Conclusions: (1) No dancer is a coward. (2) Some artists are dancers. Which conclusion(s) follow(s)?
explanation: Dancers are a subset of artists, and no artist is a coward, so no dancer is a coward (1). Since all dancers are artists, some artists are dancers (2). Both follow.
subject: CSAT

question: If '+' means division, '-' means multiplication, 'x' means addition and 'div' means subtraction, then what is the value of 18 + 6 - 4 x 3 div 2?
explanation: Replacing the symbols gives 18 / 6 x 4 + 3 - 2. Evaluating: 18/6 = 3, 3x4 = 12, 12 + 3 - 2 = 13.
subject: CSAT

question: Question: Among five boys A, B, C, D and E, who is the tallest? Statement I: A is taller than both B and C. Statement II: D is taller than A, and E is shorter than C. Which statement(s) is/are sufficient to answer?
options: (b) Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone
(d) Even both statements together are not sufficient
explanation: I alone cannot rank D; II alone does not fix B's place. Together: D > A > B, C and C > E, so D is taller than everyone - D is the tallest. Hence both together, neither alone.
subject: CSAT

question: A cube painted red on all its faces is cut into 64 identical smaller cubes (4 x 4 x 4). How many of the small cubes have exactly two faces painted?
explanation: Cubes with exactly two painted faces lie along the edges but not at the corners. Each of the 12 edges contributes (4 - 2) = 2 such cubes, giving 12 x 2 = 24.
subject: CSAT

question:
Study the following data and answer the question.

Examination data across five centres - Appeared / Qualified: P 1200/480; Q 800/360; R 1500/525; S 1000/460; T 1100/385.

Question: Which centre recorded the highest pass percentage (qualified as a percentage of those who appeared)?
explanation: Pass percentages are P 40%, Q 45%, R 35%, S 46%, T 35%. Centre S is highest at 460/1000 = 46%.
subject: CSAT

question:
Study the following data and answer the question.

Examination data across five centres - Appeared / Qualified: P 1200/480; Q 800/360; R 1500/525; S 1000/460; T 1100/385.

Question: What is the ratio of the number of candidates who qualified at centre P to the number who qualified at centre Q?
explanation: Qualified P : Q = 480 : 360 = 4 : 3.
subject: CSAT

question:
Study the following data and answer the question.

Examination data across five centres - Appeared / Qualified: P 1200/480; Q 800/360; R 1500/525; S 1000/460; T 1100/385.

Question: The overall pass percentage taking all five centres together is closest to:
explanation: Total qualified = 2210, total appeared = 5600; 2210/5600 = 39.46%, i.e. about 39.5%.
subject: CSAT

question:
Study the following data and answer the question.

A family's monthly budget of Rs 60,000 is split as Rent 30%, Food 25%, Education 15%, Transport 10%, Savings 12%, Miscellaneous 8%.

Question: How much more does the family spend on Rent than on Education each month?
explanation: Rent = 30% of 60,000 = 18,000; Education = 15% = 9,000; difference = Rs 9,000.
subject: CSAT

question:
Study the following data and answer the question.

A family's monthly budget of Rs 60,000 is split as Rent 30%, Food 25%, Education 15%, Transport 10%, Savings 12%, Miscellaneous 8%.

Question: The amount spent on Food and Transport together is what fraction of the total monthly budget?
explanation: Food + Transport = 25% + 10% = 35% = 35/100 = 7/20 of the budget.
subject: CSAT

question:
Study the following data and answer the question.

Production ('000 units) of factories X and Y - 2019: X40,Y30; 2020: X50,Y45; 2021: X60,Y50; 2022: X55,Y65; 2023: X70,Y80.

Question: In how many of the five years was factory Y's production greater than factory X's?
explanation: Y exceeds X only in 2022 (65 vs 55) and 2023 (80 vs 70) - two years.
subject: CSAT

question:
Study the following data and answer the question.

Production ('000 units) of factories X and Y - 2019: X40,Y30; 2020: X50,Y45; 2021: X60,Y50; 2022: X55,Y65; 2023: X70,Y80.

Question: What was the percentage increase in factory X's production from 2019 to 2023?
subject: CSAT

question:
Study the following data and answer the question.

Production ('000 units) of factories X and Y - 2019: X40,Y30; 2020: X50,Y45; 2021: X60,Y50; 2022: X55,Y65; 2023: X70,Y80.

Question: Over the five years, what is the ratio of the total production of factory X to that of factory Y?
explanation: Totals are X = 275 and Y = 270; the ratio 275 : 270 reduces to 55 : 54.
subject: CSAT

question: A shopkeeper marks an article 40% above its cost price and then allows two successive discounts of 10% and 5%. His profit percentage is closest to:
explanation: Selling price = 1.40 x 0.90 x 0.95 = 1.197 of cost, a profit of about 19.7%.
subject: CSAT

question: Find the compound interest on Rs 16,000 for 2 years at 10% per annum, compounded annually.
subject: CSAT

question: A boat covers 30 km downstream in 2 hours and the same 30 km upstream in 3 hours. What is the speed of the boat in still water?
explanation: Downstream speed = 15 km/h, upstream = 10 km/h; still-water speed = (15 + 10)/2 = 12.5 km/h.
subject: CSAT

question: The average of 11 numbers is 50. The average of the first six is 49 and that of the last six is 52. What is the sixth number?
explanation: Sum of all = 550. First six + last six = 6x49 + 6x52 = 606, which counts the sixth number twice; so it is 606 - 550 = 56.
subject: CSAT

question: The present ages of A and B are in the ratio 5 : 7. Four years from now the ratio will be 3 : 4. What is B's present age?
explanation: (5x + 4)/(7x + 4) = 3/4 gives x = 4, so B = 7 x 4 = 28 years.
subject: CSAT

question: Pipe A can fill a tank in 12 hours and pipe B in 18 hours. If both are opened together, how long will the tank take to fill?
explanation: Combined rate = 1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36 of the tank per hour, so the time is 36/5 = 7.2 hours.
subject: CSAT

question: What is the remainder when 7 raised to the power 100 is divided by 5?
explanation: 7 = 2 (mod 5) and 2^4 = 16 = 1 (mod 5). Since 100 = 4 x 25, 2^100 = 1 (mod 5), so the remainder is 1.
subject: CSAT

question: The HCF of two numbers is 12 and their LCM is 144. If one number is 36, what is the other?
explanation: Product of the numbers = HCF x LCM = 12 x 144 = 1728; the other number = 1728/36 = 48.
subject: CSAT

question: A rectangular field is 60 m long and 40 m wide. A path 5 m wide runs all around it on the inside. Find the area of the path.
explanation: Outer area = 60 x 40 = 2400; inner rectangle = 50 x 30 = 1500; path = 2400 - 1500 = 900 sq m.
subject: CSAT

question: The value of a machine depreciates by 10% each year. If its present value is Rs 50,000, what will it be worth after 2 years?
subject: CSAT

question: A and B start a business investing Rs 24,000 and Rs 36,000 respectively. After a year they make a profit of Rs 15,000. What is B's share of the profit?
explanation: Investment ratio = 24,000 : 36,000 = 2 : 3, so B's share = 3/5 x 15,000 = Rs 9,000.
subject: CSAT

question: A bag contains 4 red and 6 blue balls. Two balls are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that both are red?
subject: CSAT

question: How many terms are there in the arithmetic progression 7, 12, 17, ..., 102?
explanation: With first term 7 and common difference 5, n = (102 - 7)/5 + 1 = 19 + 1 = 20.
subject: CSAT

question: Two trains, 120 m and 130 m long, run in opposite directions at 50 km/h and 40 km/h. How long do they take to completely cross each other?
explanation: Relative speed = 90 km/h = 25 m/s; total length = 250 m; time = 250/25 = 10 seconds.
subject: CSAT

question: You are a section officer. You discover that a long-serving, well-liked colleague has been routinely inflating his travel-reimbursement claims by small amounts. The total is modest, but the practice is clearly improper. What would you do?
options: (a) Quietly speak to the colleague first, point out that the practice is improper and must stop, and report it through the proper channel if it continues.
(b) Ignore it, since the amounts are small and the colleague is popular.
(c) Immediately report him to the highest authority without any warning, to make an example of him.
(d) Begin submitting similar claims yourself, since the practice is evidently tolerated.
explanation: Addressing the wrongdoing responsibly - a private warning that allows correction, with escalation if it continues - is the balanced course. (b) condones impropriety, (c) is needlessly harsh as a first step, and (d) is itself unethical.
subject: CSAT

question: As a district officer during a severe water shortage, you have one tanker that cannot meet all demand. A wealthy locality offers to pay extra for priority supply, while a poorer locality has no alternative water source. How would you allocate the supply?
options: (a) Give priority to the wealthy locality, since the extra payment can fund future supply.
(b) Allocate primarily on the basis of need - serving the locality with no alternative source first - while drawing up an equitable schedule for the others.
(c) Distribute the water equally to every locality regardless of whether they have other sources.
(d) Refuse to decide, and let the localities settle the matter among themselves.
explanation: A scarce public resource should be allocated by need, prioritising those with no alternative while remaining equitable. (a) lets ability-to-pay override need, (c) ignores differing needs, and (d) abdicates responsibility.
subject: CSAT

question: You work in a regulatory body and learn, through confidential files, that a food product currently on sale poses a genuine health risk to consumers. Disclosing this would breach confidentiality rules. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: (a) Stay silent to honour the confidentiality rules, whatever the consequences.
(b) Leak the information anonymously to the press at once.
(c) Privately warn a few friends to avoid the product and take no further step.
(d) Promptly raise the matter internally with your superiors and the appropriate authority so that lawful, official action can be taken to protect consumers.
explanation: Escalating internally lets the organisation act officially and lawfully to protect the public. (a) places confidentiality above safety, (b) bypasses due process, and (c) is partial and ineffective.
subject: CSAT

question: An important report is due tomorrow morning. In the evening, a key member of your team requests urgent leave because of a genuine family medical emergency. What would you do?
options: (a) Refuse the leave outright; the deadline must be met at any cost.
(b) Grant the leave but make it clear that it will count against the employee's performance appraisal.
(c) Grant the leave, and manage the deadline by redistributing the remaining work, doing part of it yourself, or seeking a short extension only if truly necessary.
(d) Tell the employee to attend to the emergency and finish the report at the same time.
explanation: A humane and practical response grants the genuine emergency leave while taking concrete steps to still meet the obligation. (a) is rigid and uncaring, (b) penalises a genuine emergency, and (d) is impractical and unfair.
subject: CSAT

question: As a procurement officer evaluating bids, you receive an expensive gift from one of the bidding firms, delivered to your home before the decision is made. What is the most appropriate response?
options: (a) Accept the gift quietly; it will not influence your professional judgement.
(b) Accept the gift but award the contract to a different firm, to prove your impartiality.
(c) Keep the gift and quietly recuse yourself without telling anyone why.
(d) Return the gift, decline any such offers, and disclose the incident to your superior or the relevant committee to keep the process transparent.
explanation: Returning the gift and disclosing it preserves both the actual and the perceived integrity of the procurement. (a) creates a conflict of interest, (b) is improper and arbitrary, and (c) conceals a material fact.
subject: CSAT

question: Your superior instructs you to approve a file by skipping a mandatory verification step, calling it 'just a formality' that is delaying an urgent project. You believe skipping it is against the rules and could cause harm. What would you do?
options: (a) Comply at once, since the instruction comes from your superior.
(b) Refuse flatly and report your superior to outside authorities without any discussion.
(c) Respectfully explain why the verification matters and the risk of skipping it; if still pressed, ask for the instruction in writing and, if necessary, escalate through the proper channel.
(d) Approve the file but privately note your disagreement for your own records, and do nothing further.
explanation: The balanced response voices the concern, seeks accountability through a written instruction, and uses proper escalation - protecting both the rule and the working relationship. (a) abdicates judgement, (b) is needlessly confrontational as a first step, and (d) is passive and ineffective.
subject: CSAT
